ch26.note: Qingming (清明, “Pure Brightness”), the tomb-sweeping festival, falls about 4–5 April; families sweep the ancestral graves and burn spirit-money. In the country a temple fair (庙会) often follows, its high point a procession that carries the local deity — here a Buddhist bodhisattva — through the streets on a sedan chair amid gongs and pipes. Such fairs are a genuine folk-religion custom, though the sedan-borne procession belongs to temple festivals at large rather than to Qingming alone. Folk custom (corroborated).

Korea was a Japanese colony from 1910. In the last years of the war Japan drew Koreans into its forces on a growing scale — a volunteer scheme from 1938, then outright conscription of twenty-year-old men from December 1944 — and some two hundred thousand Koreans served, many as labor or low-grade infantry. That a garrison’s “Japanese” were really pressed Korean conscripts is thus entirely plausible. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Korea under Japanese rule”).

St. Mary’s Hall (圣玛利亚女校/女中), an elite Episcopal girls’ school in Shanghai, formally so named in 1881 and famous for its English and its wealthy pupils (the writer Eileen Chang graduated in 1937). The source prints the non-standard 圣玛丽公学院; the school’s established English name is St. Mary’s Hall. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “St. Mary’s Hall, Shanghai”).

Yuan Shikai (袁世凯, 1859–1916), the first President of the Republic of China, ruled autocratically, outlawed the Nationalist Party after the failed “Second Revolution” of 1913, and in 1915–16 tried to make himself emperor. His regime jailed and killed political opponents; that Su Lina’s revolutionary parents died in one of his prisons sets her orphaning in those years. Historical (corroborated: Encyclopædia Britannica, “Yuan Shikai”).

ch26.anchor: throwing down his pen for the army
ch26.note: The phrase renders 投笔从戎, “to throw down the writing-brush and follow the army,” a set idiom for a scholar who quits his studies to soldier. It alludes to the Later Han general Ban Chao (32–102 CE), who is said to have flung down his copyist’s brush, declaring that a man should win honor in far countries rather than grow old over documents. The allusive image is lost in plain English; the note keeps it. Literary allusion (corroborated).

ch26.anchor: the Xuefeng Mountain campaign at Zhijiang
ch26.note: The Battle of West Hunan, or Battle of the Xuefeng Mountains (雪峰山战役, 9 April–7 June 1945), turned back a Japanese drive on the airfield at Zhijiang (芷江) in western Hunan; a decisive Chinese victory, it was the last great battle of the war against Japan. Zhijiang was where the Japanese sued for surrender that August (芷江受降). Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Battle of West Hunan”).

ch26.anchor: a history student at Nanhua University
ch26.note: No university named Nanhua (南华大学) existed in wartime Republican China; institutions of that name are of much later date (a Taiwan university founded 1996; a Hunan university formed by merger in 2000). The company commander’s alma mater has no identifiable wartime referent and appears to be the author’s invention or an anachronism. Uncorroborated as a historical institution (checked: Wikipedia, “Nanhua University”; “National Southwestern Associated University”).

The headman (保长) was the lowest official of the baojia (保甲) system, an old scheme of household registration and collective responsibility revived by the Nationalists: households were grouped into jia and jia into bao, each under a headman answerable for taxes, labor levies, and reporting on his neighbors. Historical (Republican local control).

ch26.anchor: half a silver dollar for every household
ch26.note: The silver dollar (大洋, “big ocean,” i.e. the silver yuan / 银元) was the hard coin of Republican China, worth far more than the collapsing paper notes; half a dollar per household on a postman’s round was a modest but real fee. Historical (money).

ch27.anchor: routed from the Yangtze defense line
ch27.note: In April 1949 the People’s Liberation Army forced the Yangtze in the Crossing-the-River Campaign, breaking the Nationalists’ river line and taking Nanjing; Shanghai fell after a fortnight’s fighting in late May 1949. The rout pouring into the city here is that collapse. Historical (the 1949 Yangtze crossing and Shanghai campaigns).

Tilanqiao Prison (提篮桥监狱), built 1901–03 in the International Settlement and once among the largest prisons in the world (“the Alcatraz of the Orient”), known in English as Ward Road Gaol. After 1945 it held Japanese war criminals and Chinese collaborators of the Wang Jingwei regime; a U.S. military court sat inside it in 1946. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Tilanqiao Prison”).

ch27.anchor: a member of the anti-war league
ch27.note: The Japanese People’s Anti-war Alliance (日本人民反战同盟) was formed in December 1939 at Guilin, largely from captured Japanese soldiers who had turned against the war, under the writer Kaji Wataru; a parallel body, the Japanese People’s Emancipation League under Nosaka Sanzo, re-educated prisoners at Yan’an from 1944. Itō’s claim to have joined in 1944 is his passport under the new order. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Japanese People’s Anti-war Alliance”).

ch27.anchor: toll the bell for the day
ch27.note: A rendering of the proverb 做一天和尚撞一天钟, “a monk for a day tolls the bell for a day” — to do one’s work perfunctorily, drifting through each day with no thought for the next. The postmaster means the office may close at any time. Idiom (corroborated: 汉典).

The Waibaidu Bridge (外白渡桥), known in English as the Garden Bridge, spans Suzhou Creek at its mouth beside the Bund; the present steel truss, opened in 1908, was the first all-steel bridge in China. The name means the “outer toll-free ford.” Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Waibaidu Bridge”).

The China Merchants Steam Navigation Company (轮船招商局, founded 1872 by Li Hongzhang) was China’s first modern steamship line, an “officially supervised, merchant-managed” enterprise with wharves and godowns along the Huangpu. Its riverside warehouses were prizes in the street fighting for Shanghai. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “China Merchants Group”).

ch28.note: The Five-Starred Red Flag (五星红旗) was adopted on 27 September 1949 and first raised over Tiananmen on 1 October 1949, at the founding of the People’s Republic. Flying everywhere on “the first day of the new year,” it dates the scene to New Year 1950. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Flag of China”).

ch28.anchor: going up and down the streets in a green hat
ch28.note: The joke turns on 戴绿帽子, “to wear a green hat,” Chinese slang for a man whose wife is unfaithful — a cuckold. The postmen’s new green caps make them, in the ribald phrase, walking cuckolds. The idiom’s exact origin is disputed (green long marked low or brothel status), but its cuckold sense is old and universally understood; the pun cannot survive a literal English rendering. Idiom (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Green hat”).

Shilin cloth (士林布) is cotton dyed with Indanthren, a German synthetic vat-dye famed for not fading; indanthrene blue was everywhere in 1930s–40s China, in gowns and school uniforms alike — “the cloth that never fades.” On Su Lina, once queen of the dance, the plain faded stuff marks how far she has fallen. Historical (material culture; corroborated).

The exchange marks a real change of address. Nationalist and warlord armies called a superior 长官 (zhǎngguān, “officer”); the Communist forces used 首长 (shǒuzhǎng, “chief”), tied to their doctrine of equality between officers and men, 长官 carrying for them a taint of high-handedness. Su Lina, asking for a 长官, is corrected into the new vocabulary. Historical (corroborated).

ch28.anchor: on the way back to the Soviet area
ch28.note: The Soviet area (苏区) meant the base regions held by the Communists and their armies — here a rear district the underground was withdrawing to. Suqian (宿迁) is a town in northern Jiangsu. Historical (Communist base areas).

ch29.note: Pan Hannian (潘汉年, 1906–1977) was the Communists’ foremost intelligence officer in the Shanghai underground — the very world of these stories — and, after 1949, a Deputy Mayor of Shanghai. In 1955 he was suddenly arrested and accused of secret dealings with the Japanese and with the traitor Wang Jingwei; he was imprisoned and died in disgrace in 1977, and only in 1982 was the case declared a fabricated miscarriage of justice. That Zhongliang appeals to him to lift a false treason charge from his wife is bitterly ironic. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Pan Hannian”).

Chen Yi (陈毅, 1901–1972), one of the ten Marshals of the People’s Republic, was the first mayor of Shanghai after its capture in 1949 and later China’s foreign minister. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Chen Yi (marshal)”).

ch29.anchor: Luo Ruiqing, the Minister of Public Security
ch29.note: Luo Ruiqing (罗瑞卿, 1906–1978), a senior PLA general, was the first Minister of Public Security of the People’s Republic, appointed in October 1949. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Luo Ruiqing”).

ch29.anchor: the first National Day of New China
ch29.note: National Day (国庆节) falls on 1 October, the anniversary of the founding of the People’s Republic on 1 October 1949; the “first National Day” is thus that of 1 October 1950, dating Zhou Chukang’s visit to the autumn of 1950. Historical.

Pasting matchboxes at home was classic piece-work handed out through the neighborhood (street) committees of the early People’s Republic, often to those without regular jobs or under a political cloud — as Su Lina, a marked “spy suspect,” is. The detail measures her reduced life. Social custom (early PRC).

ch29.anchor: airlifted from India to Shanghai to take the surrender
ch29.note: After Japan’s surrender in August 1945, United States aircraft ferried Nationalist troops — among them forces of the Chinese Expeditionary Force returning from the India–Burma theater — to the coastal cities to accept the Japanese surrender before the Communists could reach them. Historical (the 1945 airlift to reoccupy the east).

Siping (四平), a rail city in the Northeast, was fought over repeatedly in the civil war of 1946–48. To “lead his men over” renders 起义, the battlefield defection of a Nationalist unit to the Communist side, a standard event of those years. Zhou Chukang’s Fourth Field Army (第四野战军, Lin Biao’s army, grown from the Northeast forces) went on to sweep south. Historical (corroborated: Wikipedia, “Battle of Siping”).

ch29.anchor: the first deputy division commander of the Volunteer Army to fall on the Korean battlefield
ch29.note: The Chinese People’s Volunteer Army entered the Korean War in October 1950. The claim that Zhou Chukang was the first deputy division commander (副师长) to die there is the novel’s own; standard accounts single out division chiefs of staff, not deputy commanders — Hu Qianxiu (胡乾秀), chief of staff of the 58th Division, killed at Chosin on 20 December 1950, is usually named the earliest senior officer lost. Rendered faithfully; the specific “first” is uncorroborated (checked against Chinese accounts of PVA officers killed in Korea).

ch30.note: The detail is left unexplained, but its resonance would be plain to a Chinese reader: “twenty years later” places the scene around 1970, in the Cultural Revolution (1966–76), when those denounced at struggle-sessions were commonly shaved — often the humiliating half-shaved “yin-yang head.” Su Lina, forever tainted as a former spy and a collaborator’s mistress, is destroyed in that last persecution. The reading is strongly implied rather than stated. Historical resonance.

蝇头小楷, literally “fly’s-head small regular script,” is the term for minutely fine 小楷 (small standard-script) calligraphy. It recalls the bookish, copperplate-loving Zhongliang of the story’s opening, now writing his dead wife letters no one will read. Idiom / nuance (corroborated).

潘汉年.note: Pan Hannian (1906–1977), the Communists’ chief intelligence officer in Shanghai and a Deputy Mayor of the city after 1949; purged in 1955, died in prison in 1977, rehabilitated 1982. Historical.

陈毅.note: Chen Yi (1901–1972), PLA marshal, first mayor of Shanghai after 1949 and later foreign minister. Historical.

罗瑞卿.note: Luo Ruiqing (1906–1978), a senior PLA general and the first Minister of Public Security of the People’s Republic. Historical.

杨复纲.note: Mr. Pan’s true name, revealed after his death; a martyr killed near Suqian in 1942. A fictional character; pinyin.

陈科长.note: The public-security section chief who interrogates and at last releases Su Lina and Zhongliang after 1949. A fictional character; surname romanized. Distinct from Chen Taining and from Chen Yi.

尤可常.note: The Chinese name taken by the former Japanese agent Itō Kinji after the war, when he stays on as the post office doorman. A fictional character; pinyin.

圣玛丽公学院.note: The elite Episcopal girls’ school in Shanghai (properly 圣玛利亚女校, St. Mary’s Hall, so named 1881); Su Lina’s school. The source’s 圣玛丽公学院 is a non-standard form. Historical.

招商局.note: The China Merchants Steam Navigation Company (轮船招商局, founded 1872), China’s first modern steamship line; its Huangpu warehouses are fought over in the taking of Shanghai. Historical.

反战同盟.note: The Japanese People’s Anti-war Alliance (日本人民反战同盟, formed 1939 under Kaji Wataru from Japanese prisoners of war); Itō claims membership to explain his survival. Historical.

四野.note: The Fourth Field Army (第四野战军) of the PLA, Lin Biao’s army grown out of the Northeast forces; so renamed in 1949. Historical.

提篮桥.note: Tilanqiao Prison (built 1901–03), known in English as Ward Road Gaol; after 1945 it held collaborators and Japanese war criminals. Historical.

外白渡桥.note: The steel bridge (opened 1908) over Suzhou Creek at the Bund, known in English as the Garden Bridge. Historical.

士林布.note: Cotton dyed with Indanthren, the German synthetic vat-dye prized for not fading; ubiquitous in 1930s–40s China. Historical.
